title: C#: Cache Array/Vector/String memory alignment information at startup
body:
PR #105928 fixed some problematic memory alignment assumptions that the C# size getters for Array/Vector/String were making. 

However, the fix relies on native calls on every access to the Size getter, which is in itself a problem given that these properties are automatically accessed by the runtime for most array operations, and therefore these accesses are assumed by the runtime to be a fastpath without (significant) side effects. Native calls incur a transition frame which signals to the GC that it can potentially do a collection and/or move memory around, which is definitely not a side-effect-free scenario and not a safe or performant thing to do in getters that can be accessed multiple times per-object per-frame.

This PR restores the previous math logic for calculating memory offsets which mirrors the native math in cowdata.h, but using native memory aligment information that is sent once during initialization from native to managed land and then cached, since this information never changes. This ensures that these properties always return the same as their native counterparts without incurring interop costs.

In the process of setting up the marshaling data initialization, I've refactored the various .net hostfxr/coreclr/nativeaot initialization methods to be the consistent with each other (taking the same inputs and outputs).

The marshaling data initialization path on the C# side is on a separate method because the general init method already has a lot of parameters. which are different depending on whether it's an editor or template build, and the marshaling data method could potentially change more often than the rest of the init code, if the cowdata.h offsets are changed (as has already happened from 4.5 to 4.6), so maintenance-wise it's better to keep them separate.

/cc @Ivorforce, this is the change I was talking about in the C# doc comments





### Benchmarks

The `Godot.Collections.Array` is a class wrapper around the `godot_array` struct that implements C# collection interfaces. Its `IndexOf` has a special case for when the collection is empty, so it can avoid the cost of an interop call. To check if the underlying native array is empty, it uses its `Count` property, which in turn calls the `Size` property of the wrapped `godot_array` struct.

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/26228372b9a3d766058f886d390293c3592bac6d/modules/mono/glue/GodotSharp/GodotSharp/Core/Array.cs#L741-L747

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/26228372b9a3d766058f886d390293c3592bac6d/modules/mono/glue/GodotSharp/GodotSharp/Core/Array.cs#L901

With current master, `Size` triggers an interop call, while in this PR it doesn't. This difference makes this codepath particularly amenable to seeing the impact of interop calls in a fairly isolated way.

I could have just called `Count` directly, of course, but using `IndexOf()` illustrates the sort of reliance that methods have on the speed of property getters, and the impact that surprise side effects can have on seemingly unrelated methods. These types of methods are required interface implementations that often rely on replicating existing upstream dotnet/runtime implementations of the standard collection classes, and the upstream performance assumptions of property getters are brought along with them.

This benchmark tracks the time spent on the following loop with 1 million iterations, with an empty list:

```
Godot.Collections.Array<int> list = new();
for (var i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++)
{
    // force a call to Count
    _ = list.IndexOf(0);
}
```

Idle is the time reported by godot-benchmarks that is being spent on process calls.

| Scenario | PR (idle) | Master (idle) | Diff | Diff% |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| IndexOf | 30.12ms | 43.99ms | -13.87ms | -46% |


This test is running on the draw callback, every frame, for 10 seconds.
